content.title: Welcome to n8n — The Automation Powerhouse
content.explanation:
Imagine you spend 2 hours every morning reading emails, copying data into spreadsheets, sending Slack messages, and updating your CRM. What if a robot did all of that in 2 seconds while you slept?

**That robot is n8n.**

n8n (pronounced 'n-eight-n') is an open-source workflow automation platform that lets you connect apps, services, and APIs together — without writing much code. Think of it as building a conveyor belt in a factory: data enters from one side, gets processed, transformed, and routed to the right destination automatically.

**Why 'n8n'?**
The name stands for **nodemation** (node + automation). Every step in your workflow is a 'node' — a building block that does one specific thing. You connect nodes together to create powerful automated workflows.

**Real Numbers:**
- 400+ built-in integrations (Gmail, Slack, OpenAI, Google Sheets, Notion, and more)
- 1M+ workflows created by the community
- Used by companies from startups to enterprises
- Self-hosted or cloud — you choose

**What makes n8n different from Zapier or Make?**

| Feature | n8n | Zapier | Make |
|---------|-----|--------|------|
| Open Source | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | ❌ No |
| Self-Hosted | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | ❌ No |
| Code Node | ✅ Full JS/Python | ❌ Limited | ⚠️ Basic |
| AI Integration | ✅ Native | ⚠️ Add-on | ⚠️ Add-on |
| Pricing | Free (self-hosted) | $20+/mo | $9+/mo |
| Complex Logic | ✅ Branching, loops | ⚠️ Limited | ✅ Good |

**Bottom line:** n8n gives you the power of code with the simplicity of drag-and-drop. You get full control, full transparency, and zero vendor lock-in.
content.tip: n8n is especially powerful for AI engineers because it has native OpenAI, LangChain, and vector database nodes — making it the best platform for building AI-powered automations.

content.title: Low-Code vs No-Code — Where Does n8n Fit?
content.explanation:
You have probably heard the terms 'no-code' and 'low-code' thrown around. Let's clarify what they mean and where n8n sits:

**No-Code Platforms** (e.g., Zapier, Airtable)
- Zero coding required
- Simple drag-and-drop
- Limited flexibility — you can only do what the platform allows
- Great for non-technical users

**Low-Code Platforms** (e.g., n8n, Retool)
- Mostly visual drag-and-drop
- CAN write code when needed (JavaScript, Python)
- Much more flexible — you can customize everything
- Great for developers AND non-developers

**Full-Code** (e.g., writing Python scripts from scratch)
- Maximum flexibility
- Requires programming expertise
- Takes longer to build
- Full control over everything

**n8n is the perfect 'low-code' sweet spot:**
- 90% of the time, you drag and drop nodes — no coding needed
- 10% of the time, you write a few lines of JavaScript in a Code Node for custom logic
- You get the speed of no-code WITH the power of full code

**Why this matters for AI Automation:**
When building AI automations, you often need to parse complex API responses, transform data structures, or implement custom logic. Pure no-code tools hit a wall. n8n lets you break through that wall with its Code Node while keeping everything visual and manageable.
content.tip: Think of n8n as 'Visual Programming'. You see the entire data flow on a canvas, but you can zoom into any node and write custom code when the visual tools are not enough.

content.title: n8n Cloud vs Self-Hosted — Which Should You Choose?
content.explanation:
n8n offers two ways to run the platform. Let's break down each:

**☁️ n8n Cloud (Managed Service)**
- n8n hosts everything for you
- No server setup required
- Automatic updates and backups
- Starts at $20/month (Starter plan)
- Best for: Beginners, small teams, quick prototyping

**🖥️ Self-Hosted (You Run It)**
- You install n8n on your own server
- Full control over data and security
- Completely free (open source)
- Requires Docker or npm knowledge
- Best for: Developers, privacy-sensitive data, cost optimization

**Quick Decision Matrix:**

| Factor | Cloud | Self-Hosted |
|--------|-------|-------------|
| Setup Time | 2 minutes | 15-30 minutes |
| Cost | $20+/month | Free (+ server costs) |
| Maintenance | n8n handles it | You handle it |
| Data Privacy | n8n servers | Your servers |
| Custom Nodes | Limited | Unlimited |
| Scalability | Auto-scaled | You manage |
| Best For | Learning, small teams | Production, enterprises |

**Our Recommendation for This Course:**
Start with **n8n Cloud** (free trial available) to learn without friction. Once you are comfortable, set up a self-hosted instance with Docker for production workflows.

**Important:** Both options use the exact same interface and features. Everything you learn on Cloud works identically on self-hosted, and vice versa.
content.tip: If you are following this course to learn, use n8n Cloud first. You can always migrate to self-hosted later — n8n lets you export and import workflows easily.

content.title: Three Ways to Install n8n
content.explanation:
There are three main ways to get n8n running. We will cover all of them so you can choose the best option for your situation.

**Method 1: n8n Cloud (Easiest — 2 minutes)**
Sign up at https://n8n.io and start using n8n instantly in your browser. No installation needed. Best for learning and quick prototyping.

**Method 2: npm (For Node.js developers)**
Install n8n as a global npm package. Requires Node.js 18+ installed on your machine.

```bash
# Install n8n globally
npm install n8n -g

# Start n8n
n8n start
```

After running `n8n start`, open your browser and go to `http://localhost:5678`. That is your n8n instance!

**Method 3: Docker (Recommended for production)**
Run n8n in a Docker container. This is the most reliable method for production deployments.

```bash
# Pull and run n8n with Docker
docker run -it --rm \
  --name n8n \
  -p 5678:5678 \
  -v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n \
  docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n
```

This command:
- `-p 5678:5678` — Maps port 5678 so you can access n8n in your browser
- `-v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n` — Persists your data so workflows survive container restarts

**Which should you use right now?**
- If you want to start learning immediately → **n8n Cloud**
- If you have Node.js installed → **npm**
- If you know Docker → **Docker**
content.tip: For this course, we recommend starting with n8n Cloud to focus on learning workflows, not infrastructure. You can always switch to self-hosted later.

content.title: Docker Compose Setup — The Professional Way
content.explanation:
For production deployments, Docker Compose is the gold standard. It lets you define your entire n8n stack (n8n + database + reverse proxy) in a single file.

**Create a `docker-compose.yml` file:**

```yaml
version: '3.8'

services:
  n8n:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n
    restart: always
    ports:
      - '5678:5678'
    environment:
      - N8N_BASIC_AUTH_ACTIVE=true
      - N8N_BASIC_AUTH_USER=admin
      - N8N_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD=your-secure-password
      - N8N_HOST=localhost
      - N8N_PORT=5678
      - N8N_PROTOCOL=http
      - GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata
      - TZ=Asia/Kolkata
      - DB_TYPE=sqlite
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n

volumes:
  n8n_data:
```

**Start it with:**
```bash
docker-compose up -d
```

**Key Environment Variables:**

| Variable | Purpose | Example |
|----------|---------|--------|
| `N8N_BASIC_AUTH_ACTIVE` | Enable login protection | `true` |
| `N8N_BASIC_AUTH_USER` | Login username | `admin` |
| `N8N_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD` | Login password | `securePass123` |
| `GENERIC_TIMEZONE` | Set your timezone | `Asia/Kolkata` |
| `DB_TYPE` | Database type | `sqlite` or `postgresdb` |
| `N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Encrypt stored credentials | Any random string |

**For PostgreSQL (production-grade):**
Replace `DB_TYPE=sqlite` with PostgreSQL configuration for better performance at scale:
```
DB_TYPE=postgresdb
DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST=postgres
DB_POSTGRESDB_PORT=5432
DB_POSTGRESDB_DATABASE=n8n
DB_POSTGRESDB_USER=n8n
DB_POSTGRESDB_PASSWORD=n8n
```
content.tip: Always set N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY in production. Without it, your stored API keys and credentials are not encrypted at rest.

content.title: Updating n8n and Backup Strategies
content.explanation:
Keeping n8n updated is important for security patches and new features. Here is how to update for each installation method:

**npm Update:**
```bash
npm update n8n -g
```

**Docker Update:**
```bash
# Pull the latest image
docker pull docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n

# Restart the container
docker-compose down
docker-compose up -d
```

**n8n Cloud:**
Updates happen automatically — you do not need to do anything!

---

**Backup Strategies:**

Your n8n data includes workflows, credentials, execution history, and settings. Losing this data means rebuilding everything from scratch.

**Method 1: Export Workflows (Manual)**
- Go to each workflow → Menu → Download as JSON
- Store the JSON files in a Git repository
- Best for: Version control and collaboration

**Method 2: Volume Backup (Docker)**
```bash
# Backup the n8n data volume
docker run --rm -v n8n_data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup \
  alpine tar czf /backup/n8n-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz /data
```

**Method 3: Database Backup (PostgreSQL)**
```bash
pg_dump -U n8n -d n8n > n8n-backup.sql
```

**Backup Schedule Recommendation:**
- Daily: Automated database/volume backups
- Weekly: Full workflow exports to Git
- Before updates: Always backup before upgrading n8n
content.tip: Create a backup workflow inside n8n itself! Use a Schedule Trigger to auto-export all workflows to Google Drive or S3 every night.

content.title: Workflows — The Heart of n8n
content.explanation:
A **workflow** is a sequence of automated steps that accomplish a task. Think of it like a recipe:

- A recipe has ingredients (data) and steps (nodes)
- Each step transforms the ingredients in some way
- The final result is a finished dish (automated outcome)

**Workflow Components:**

**1. Trigger Node (The Starting Point)**
Every workflow begins with a trigger. The trigger answers the question: 'When should this workflow run?'
- On a schedule (every hour, every morning at 9 AM)
- When something happens (new email received, form submitted)
- When manually clicked (for testing)

**2. Nodes (The Steps)**
Each node performs one action:
- Fetch data from an API
- Send an email
- Update a spreadsheet
- Process data with AI
- Make a decision (if/else)

**3. Connections (The Wires)**
Connections are the lines between nodes. They define:
- The order of execution (which node runs first)
- The data flow (what data passes from one node to the next)

**4. Data (The Information)**
Data flows through the workflow as JSON objects. Each node:
- Receives input data from the previous node
- Processes or transforms that data
- Sends output data to the next node
content.tip: A workflow can be as simple as 2 nodes (trigger → action) or as complex as 50+ nodes with branches, loops, and error handling. Start simple and add complexity as needed.

content.title: Workflow Lifecycle
content.explanation: Every workflow follows this lifecycle: you create it, build it with nodes and connections, test it, fix any issues, then activate it to run automatically. After activation, you monitor it through the Executions page.

content.title: Execution Order and Data Flow
content.explanation:
Understanding how data flows through a workflow is crucial for building reliable automations.

**Execution Order:**
n8n executes nodes from left to right, following the connections. If a node has multiple outputs (like an IF node), only the matching branch executes.

```
Trigger → Node A → Node B → Node C
                         ↘ Node D (branch)
```

In this example:
1. Trigger fires
2. Node A runs, output goes to Node B
3. Node B runs, output goes to Node C AND Node D
4. Node C and Node D run (if connected)

**Input vs Output:**
Every node has:
- **Input**: The data it receives from the previous node
- **Output**: The data it produces after processing

You can see both by clicking on a node after execution. The left panel shows input, the right panel shows output.

**Items:**
n8n processes data as 'items'. If a node receives 5 items (e.g., 5 emails), it processes each one. This is like a loop — the node runs its logic on each item individually.

Example:
```json
[
  { "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com" },
  { "name": "Bob", "email": "bob@example.com" },
  { "name": "Charlie", "email": "charlie@example.com" }
]
```
If this data flows into a Gmail node, it will send 3 separate emails — one to each person.
content.example: Input (3 items) → Gmail Node → Output (3 emails sent)

content.title: Workflow Best Practices
content.explanation:
Before you start building, learn these best practices that will save you hours of debugging:

**1. Name Everything Clearly**
- Bad: 'HTTP Request', 'IF', 'Code'
- Good: 'Fetch Customer Data', 'Is VIP Customer?', 'Calculate Discount'
- Why: When you have 20 nodes, clear names tell you what each one does at a glance

**2. Add Sticky Notes**
Use sticky notes on the canvas to document:
- What the workflow does
- Why certain decisions were made
- Input/output format expectations

**3. Test Incrementally**
Do NOT build 15 nodes and then test. Instead:
- Add 1-2 nodes → Test → Verify output
- Add the next node → Test → Verify
- This way, when something breaks, you know exactly which node caused it

**4. Use Error Handling**
Always add error handling for nodes that call external APIs:
- APIs can be down
- Rate limits can be hit
- Data format can change
We will cover error handling in detail in Lesson 2.17.

**5. Keep Workflows Focused**
One workflow = One job. If a workflow does too many unrelated things, split it into smaller workflows that call each other.

**6. Version Your Workflows**
Export your workflows as JSON regularly. Store them in Git. This gives you a history of changes and the ability to roll back.
content.tip: The #1 mistake beginners make is building a huge workflow without testing. Always test after adding each node. It takes 5 seconds and saves you 5 hours of debugging.

content.title: Manual Trigger, Execute, Save, and Activate
content.explanation:
Four essential actions you will use every day in n8n:

**▶️ Manual Trigger**
The 'Manual Trigger' node lets you run a workflow by clicking a button. Perfect for testing.
- Every new workflow starts with a Manual Trigger by default
- You can replace it with a Schedule, Webhook, or other trigger later
- During development, always keep a Manual Trigger so you can test easily

**🔄 Execute Workflow**
Click the play button (▶️) in the toolbar to run the workflow once.
- This is called a 'manual execution'
- All nodes run in order
- You can see the output data of each node
- Use this for testing and debugging

**💾 Save Workflow**
Press `Ctrl+S` or click the save button. Important:
- n8n does NOT auto-save by default
- If you close the browser without saving, your changes are lost
- Get in the habit of saving after every change

**✅ Activate Workflow**
The activate toggle (top right) switches the workflow from 'inactive' to 'active'.
- **Inactive**: The workflow only runs when you manually click Execute
- **Active**: The workflow runs automatically based on its trigger
- Example: If you have a Schedule Trigger set to 9 AM, the workflow only runs at 9 AM if it is activated

**Important:** A workflow MUST be active for its trigger to fire automatically. This is the #1 confusion for beginners — they build a workflow, wonder why it is not running, and realize they forgot to activate it.
content.tip: Keyboard shortcut: Ctrl+S to save. Use it religiously. You will thank yourself later.

content.title: Triggers — What Starts Your Workflow
content.explanation:
A **Trigger** is the 'when' of your workflow. It defines the event that starts the automation. Without a trigger, a workflow just sits there doing nothing.

**Every workflow must have exactly one trigger node** (placed at the very beginning).

Here are the most important trigger types in n8n:

**1. Manual Trigger**
- Runs when you click 'Execute'
- Used for testing and one-off tasks
- No configuration needed

**2. Schedule Trigger** ⏰
- Runs on a time-based schedule
- Options: Every X minutes, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, cron expression
- Example: Every Monday at 9 AM, every 15 minutes

**3. Webhook Trigger** 🌐
- Runs when an external service sends data to a URL
- n8n gives you a unique URL — anyone who sends data to that URL triggers the workflow
- Example: A website form submission, a payment notification, a GitHub event

**4. Form Trigger** 📝
- Creates a web form that users can fill out
- When submitted, the form data enters the workflow
- No external form builder needed

**5. Email Trigger (IMAP)** 📧
- Monitors an email inbox
- Triggers when a new email arrives
- Can filter by sender, subject, or folder

content.title: More Trigger Types and When to Use Each
content.explanation:
**6. App-Specific Triggers**
n8n has dedicated triggers for popular services:

| Trigger | When It Fires |
|---------|---------------|
| Slack Trigger | New message in a channel |
| Google Drive Trigger | File uploaded or modified |
| GitHub Trigger | New commit, PR, or issue |
| Telegram Trigger | New message to your bot |
| Airtable Trigger | New or updated record |
| Google Sheets Trigger | New row added |

**7. Database Triggers**
- PostgreSQL Trigger: Fires when rows change
- MySQL Trigger: Fires on INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE

**Which Trigger Should You Use?**

| Scenario | Best Trigger |
|----------|-------------|
| Run every morning at 9 AM | Schedule Trigger |
| React to a form submission | Webhook or Form Trigger |
| Process new emails | Email Trigger (IMAP) |
| Monitor file uploads | Google Drive Trigger |
| Respond to Slack messages | Slack Trigger |
| Receive API calls from other systems | Webhook Trigger |
| Manual testing | Manual Trigger |

**Key Insight:**
The trigger determines the **shape of your input data**. A Webhook trigger gives you whatever data was sent to the URL. A Gmail trigger gives you email fields (from, subject, body). Understanding what data each trigger provides is crucial for building the rest of the workflow.
content.tip: Webhook triggers are the most versatile — any service that can send HTTP requests can trigger your workflow. This includes websites, mobile apps, IoT devices, and other automation tools.

content.title: Action Nodes — Making Things Happen
content.explanation:
If triggers are the 'when', action nodes are the 'what'. They perform the actual work in your workflow.

**The Most Important Action Nodes:**

**📧 Gmail Node**
Send, read, reply to, and manage emails.
- Actions: Send Email, Get Email, Reply to Email, Add Label, Delete Email
- Key fields: To, Subject, Body (supports HTML), Attachments
- Tip: Use expressions in the Body to create dynamic, personalized emails

**📊 Google Sheets Node**
Read, write, update, and delete spreadsheet data.
- Actions: Append Row, Read Rows, Update Row, Delete Row, Clear Sheet
- Connect to any Google Sheet using your Google credentials
- Perfect for logging data, creating reports, and managing lists

**💬 Slack Node**
Send messages, update channels, and manage Slack workspaces.
- Actions: Send Message, Update Message, Upload File, Get Channel Info
- Supports: Channel messages, DMs, threads, rich formatting (blocks)
- Tip: Use Slack Block Kit for beautiful, interactive messages

**📝 Notion Node**
Create pages, update databases, and query Notion workspaces.
- Actions: Create Page, Update Page, Get Database Items, Search
- Perfect for: Knowledge bases, task management, content planning

**🤖 OpenAI Node**
Interact with ChatGPT and other OpenAI models.
- Actions: Chat Completion, Create Image, Transcribe Audio, Embeddings
- This is your gateway to AI-powered automations
- Requires an OpenAI API key

content.title: More Action Nodes You Should Know
content.explanation:
**💬 Discord Node**
Send messages to Discord channels and manage servers.
- Actions: Send Message, Edit Message, Get Channel
- Great for: Dev team notifications, community management

**📱 Telegram Node**
Send messages, photos, and files to Telegram users or groups.
- Actions: Send Message, Send Photo, Send Document
- Create a Telegram Bot first (via @BotFather)
- Use for: Personal notifications, team alerts

**🌐 HTTP Request Node (The Universal Node)**
This is arguably the most powerful node in n8n. It can connect to ANY service that has an API.
- Supports: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE
- Authentication: API Key, Bearer Token, OAuth, Basic Auth
- Body types: JSON, Form Data, Raw
- If n8n does not have a dedicated node for a service, the HTTP Request node can fill the gap

**We will cover the HTTP Request node in depth in Lesson 2.15.**

**Quick Comparison:**

| Node | When to Use It |
|------|---------------|
| Gmail | Send/read emails |
| Google Sheets | Log data, read spreadsheets |
| Slack | Team notifications |
| Notion | Knowledge management |
| OpenAI | AI-powered processing |
| Discord | Gaming/dev community alerts |
| Telegram | Personal/bot notifications |
| HTTP Request | Any API not covered above |
content.tip: When in doubt, use the HTTP Request node. If a service has a REST API, the HTTP Request node can talk to it. It is the Swiss Army knife of n8n.

content.title: Project: AI Email Summarizer
content.explanation:
Let's build a practical workflow that showcases action nodes working together.

**What It Does:**
When a new email arrives, the workflow reads it, sends the content to OpenAI for summarization, and posts the summary to Slack.

**Workflow:**
```
Email Trigger (IMAP — new email arrives)
  ↓
OpenAI Node (Summarize the email)
  ↓
Slack Node (Post summary to #email-summaries channel)
  ↓
Gmail Node (Add 'Processed' label to the email)
```

**Node Configurations:**

**1. Email Trigger (IMAP)**
- Mailbox: INBOX
- Check every: 1 minute

**2. OpenAI Node**
- Model: gpt-4o-mini
- System Prompt: 'You are an email summarizer. Summarize the following email in 2-3 bullet points. Include the sender, main topic, and any action items.'
- User Message: `{{ $json.text }}` (the email body from the trigger)

**3. Slack Node**
- Channel: #email-summaries
- Message:
```

*From:* {{ $('Email Trigger').item.json.from }}
*Subject:* {{ $('Email Trigger').item.json.subject }}

{{ $json.message.content }}
```

**4. Gmail Node**
- Action: Add Label
- Label: 'AI-Processed'
- Message ID: from the Email Trigger output

This workflow saves you from reading every email. AI reads them for you and posts summaries where your team can see them.

content.title: JSON — The Language of n8n Data
content.explanation:
Every piece of data in n8n is JSON (JavaScript Object Notation). If you understand JSON, you understand n8n data. Let's master it.

**What is JSON?**
JSON is a structured text format for representing data. It uses key-value pairs.

**Basic JSON Object:**
```json
{
  "name": "Alice",
  "email": "alice@example.com",
  "age": 28,
  "isVIP": true
}
```

**Key Rules:**
- Keys are always strings in double quotes: `"name"`
- Values can be: strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, or nested objects
- Key-value pairs are separated by commas
- Objects are wrapped in `{ }`
- Arrays are wrapped in `[ ]`

**JSON Array (Multiple Items):**
```json
[
  { "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com" },
  { "name": "Bob", "email": "bob@example.com" },
  { "name": "Charlie", "email": "charlie@example.com" }
]
```

**Nested Objects:**
```json
{
  "customer": {
    "name": "Alice",
    "address": {
      "city": "Mumbai",
      "country": "India"
    },
    "orders": [
      { "id": 1, "total": 150 },
      { "id": 2, "total": 300 }
    ]
  }
}
```

To access the city: `customer.address.city` → `"Mumbai"`
To access the first order total: `customer.orders[0].total` → `150`

content.title: Items — How n8n Processes Data
content.explanation:
In n8n, data flows between nodes as **items**. Each item is one JSON object.

**Single Item:**
When an HTTP Request node fetches weather data, it returns 1 item:
```json
[
  {
    "json": {
      "temperature": 28,
      "humidity": 65,
      "description": "Partly cloudy"
    }
  }
]
```

**Multiple Items:**
When a Google Sheets node reads 3 rows, it returns 3 items:
```json
[
  { "json": { "name": "Alice", "score": 95 } },
  { "json": { "name": "Bob", "score": 82 } },
  { "json": { "name": "Charlie", "score": 78 } }
]
```

**Why Items Matter:**
When a node receives multiple items, it processes EACH item separately. This is like an automatic loop.

Example: If 3 items flow into a Gmail node configured to send an email:
- Item 1 → Email to Alice
- Item 2 → Email to Bob
- Item 3 → Email to Charlie

**You do NOT need to write a loop manually.** n8n does it for you.

**Accessing Item Data:**
Inside any node, you access the current item's data using:
- `{{ $json.name }}` → The 'name' field of the current item
- `{{ $json.score }}` → The 'score' field of the current item

We will learn more about these expressions in the next lesson.
content.tip: Click on any node after execution to see its items. The left shows input items, the right shows output items. Use the 'Table' view for a spreadsheet-like display.

content.title: Practice: Reading and Passing Data
content.explanation:
Let's practice reading JSON and understanding how data flows between nodes.

**Scenario:** You fetch customer data from an API. The response is:

```json
{
  "customers": [
    {
      "id": 101,
      "name": "Priya Sharma",
      "email": "priya@techcorp.com",
      "plan": "premium",
      "monthly_spend": 4500
    },
    {
      "id": 102,
      "name": "Rahul Patel",
      "email": "rahul@startup.io",
      "plan": "free",
      "monthly_spend": 0
    }
  ]
}
```

**Question 1:** How do you access Priya's email?
Answer: `customers[0].email` → `"priya@techcorp.com"`

**Question 2:** How do you access Rahul's plan?
Answer: `customers[1].plan` → `"free"`

**Question 3:** How many items would this produce if split?
Answer: 2 items (one per customer)

**Important Node: Split Out**
The 'Split Out' node takes an array (like `customers`) and converts it into separate items. This is how you go from 1 item containing an array to multiple items:

Before Split Out: 1 item with `customers` array (2 entries)
After Split Out: 2 separate items (one per customer)

This is essential when API responses contain arrays that you need to process individually.

content.title: Expressions — Making Workflows Dynamic
content.explanation:
Expressions are what make n8n workflows powerful. Instead of hardcoding values, you use expressions to dynamically reference data from previous nodes.

**What is an Expression?**
An expression is a piece of code wrapped in `{{ }}` that gets replaced with actual data at runtime.

**Static (Hardcoded):**
```
Subject: Daily Report
```

**Dynamic (Expression):**
```
Subject: Daily Report for {{ $now.format('MMMM d, yyyy') }}
```
Result: `Daily Report for July 6, 2026`

**The Expression Editor:**
In any node, click on a field and you will see an option to switch to 'Expression' mode (the `{ }` icon). This opens the Expression Editor where you can:
- Write expressions
- Browse available variables
- See a live preview of the result

**Essential Expression Syntax:**

| Expression | Description | Example Output |
|-----------|-------------|----------------|
| `{{ $json.name }}` | Current item field | `"Alice"` |
| `{{ $json.email }}` | Another field | `"alice@example.com"` |
| `{{ $('Node Name').item.json.field }}` | Field from a specific node | Any value from that node |
| `{{ $now }}` | Current date/time | `2026-07-06T07:30:00` |
| `{{ $execution.id }}` | Current execution ID | `"abc123"` |
| `{{ $workflow.name }}` | Workflow name | `"Daily Report"` |

content.title: Accessing Data from Previous Nodes
content.explanation:
The most common use of expressions is accessing data from previous nodes.

**From the Immediately Previous Node:**
```
{{ $json.fieldName }}
```
This accesses data from the node directly connected before the current one.

**From Any Specific Node (by name):**
```
{{ $('HTTP Request').item.json.temperature }}
```
This accesses the 'temperature' field from a node named 'HTTP Request', regardless of where it is in the chain.

**Example Workflow:**
```
Webhook → HTTP Request → Gmail
```

Inside the Gmail node:
- `{{ $json.temperature }}` → Gets data from HTTP Request (previous node)
- `{{ $('Webhook').item.json.name }}` → Gets data from Webhook (2 nodes back)

**Accessing Nested Data:**
```
{{ $json.user.address.city }}
{{ $json.orders[0].total }}
{{ $json.tags.join(', ') }}
```

**String Concatenation:**
```
{{ 'Hello ' + $json.name + ', your order #' + $json.orderId + ' is confirmed!' }}
```
Result: `Hello Alice, your order #4521 is confirmed!`

content.title: Built-in Functions: Date, Math, and String
content.explanation:
n8n provides powerful built-in functions you can use inside expressions.

**📅 Date Functions:**

| Expression | Output |
|-----------|--------|
| `{{ $now }}` | Current date/time ISO string |
| `{{ $now.format('yyyy-MM-dd') }}` | `2026-07-06` |
| `{{ $now.format('MMMM d, yyyy') }}` | `July 6, 2026` |
| `{{ $now.format('HH:mm') }}` | `13:04` |
| `{{ $now.minus(1, 'day').format('yyyy-MM-dd') }}` | Yesterday's date |
| `{{ $now.plus(7, 'days').format('yyyy-MM-dd') }}` | Date 7 days from now |
| `{{ $today }}` | Today at midnight |

**🔢 Math Functions:**

| Expression | Output |
|-----------|--------|
| `{{ $json.price * 1.18 }}` | Price + 18% GST |
| `{{ Math.round($json.score * 100) / 100 }}` | Round to 2 decimals |
| `{{ Math.max($json.a, $json.b) }}` | Larger of two values |
| `{{ Math.floor($json.price) }}` | Round down |

**📝 String Functions:**

| Expression | Output |
|-----------|--------|
| `{{ $json.name.toUpperCase() }}` | `ALICE` |
| `{{ $json.name.toLowerCase() }}` | `alice` |
| `{{ $json.email.split('@')[1] }}` | `example.com` (domain) |
| `{{ $json.text.substring(0, 100) }}` | First 100 characters |
| `{{ $json.sentence.replace('old', 'new') }}` | Replace text |
| `{{ $json.tags.join(', ') }}` | Array to comma string |
| `{{ $json.name.includes('Ali') }}` | `true` or `false` |
content.tip: The Expression Editor has autocomplete! Start typing and it will suggest available fields and functions. Use it — it prevents typos and shows you what is available.

content.explanation:

```

```

```

```

**Scenario 5: Format Currency**
```
{{ '₹' + $json.amount.toLocaleString('en-IN') }}
```
Result: `₹1,50,000`

content.title: The Edit Fields Node — Reshaping Your Data
content.explanation:
The **Edit Fields** node (also called 'Set' node) lets you reshape, rename, and transform data. It is one of the most frequently used nodes in n8n.

**When You Need It:**
- An API returns 20 fields but you only need 3
- Field names do not match what the next node expects
- You need to create new computed fields
- You want to combine data from multiple sources

**Common Operations:**

**1. Keep Only Specific Fields**
Input:
```json
{ "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@ex.com", "age": 28, "phone": "123", "address": "..." }
```
Edit Fields Config: Keep only `name` and `email`
Output:
```json
{ "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@ex.com" }
```

**2. Rename Fields**
Input: `{ "customer_name": "Alice" }`
Rename: `customer_name` → `name`
Output: `{ "name": "Alice" }`

**3. Create New Computed Fields**
Input: `{ "price": 1000, "quantity": 5 }`
New field: `total` = `{{ $json.price * $json.quantity }}`
Output: `{ "price": 1000, "quantity": 5, "total": 5000 }`

**4. Set Static Values**
Add a field with a hardcoded value:
`status` = `"processed"`
`processed_at` = `{{ $now.toISO() }}`
content.tip: Use the Edit Fields node after every API call to clean up the data before passing it to the next node. This makes your workflows easier to debug.

content.title: Project: Transform CRM Data into a Clean Report
content.explanation:
Let's build a practical data transformation workflow.

**Scenario:** Your CRM API returns messy customer data. You need to clean it up and create a formatted report in Google Sheets.

**Raw CRM Data (from HTTP Request):**
```json
{
  "cust_f_name": "Priya",
  "cust_l_name": "Sharma",
  "cust_email_addr": "priya@tech.com",
  "purchase_total_usd": 2500,
  "acct_created_ts": "2024-03-15T10:30:00Z",
  "last_login_ts": "2026-07-05T14:20:00Z",
  "internal_id": "xyz123",
  "debug_flag": false
}
```

**What We Want (Clean Data for Report):**
```json
{
  "Full Name": "Priya Sharma",
  "Email": "priya@tech.com",
  "Total Purchases (₹)": "₹2,07,500",
  "Member Since": "March 2024",
  "Status": "Active"
}
```

**Edit Fields Configuration:**
- Full Name: `{{ $json.cust_f_name + ' ' + $json.cust_l_name }}`
- Email: `{{ $json.cust_email_addr }}`
- Total Purchases (₹): `{{ '₹' + ($json.purchase_total_usd * 83).toLocaleString('en-IN') }}`
- Member Since: `{{ DateTime.fromISO($json.acct_created_ts).toFormat('MMMM yyyy') }}`
- Status: `{{ $json.last_login_ts > $now.minus(30, 'days').toISO() ? 'Active' : 'Inactive' }}`

**Workflow:**
```
Schedule Trigger (Weekly)
  ↓
HTTP Request (Fetch CRM data)
  ↓
Edit Fields (Transform and clean)
  ↓
Google Sheets (Append to report)
```

content.explanation:
In this lesson, you learned:

• The **Code Node** lets you write JavaScript/Python for custom logic

content.title: IF Node — Making Decisions
content.explanation:
Real workflows need to make decisions. The **IF node** evaluates a condition and routes data to one of two paths: **True** or **False**.

**How It Works:**
```
                    ┌─ True Branch → Send VIP Email
Data → IF Node ─────┤
                    └─ False Branch → Send Standard Email
```

**Example: VIP Customer Routing**
Condition: `{{ $json.total_spend }}` is greater than `10000`

- If total_spend > 10000 → True branch → Send VIP welcome package
- If total_spend <= 10000 → False branch → Send standard welcome email

**Condition Types:**

| Type | Example |
|------|--------|
| Number: Greater than | `$json.amount > 1000` |
| Number: Less than | `$json.quantity < 5` |
| Number: Equal | `$json.status_code == 200` |
| String: Equal | `$json.country == 'India'` |
| String: Contains | `$json.email` contains `@gmail.com` |
| Boolean: Is true | `$json.isActive` is true |
| Value: Exists | `$json.phone` exists |
| Value: Is empty | `$json.notes` is empty |

**Multiple Conditions:**
You can combine conditions with AND/OR:
- AND: Both conditions must be true
- OR: At least one condition must be true

Example: `total_spend > 10000 AND country == 'India'`
content.tip: Always connect BOTH outputs (True and False) of an IF node. If you only connect the True branch, items that fail the condition will be silently dropped.

content.title: Switch Node — Multiple Paths
content.explanation:
The **Switch node** is like a more powerful IF. Instead of just True/False, it can route data to multiple paths based on different conditions.

**When to Use Switch vs IF:**
- **IF**: Two paths (yes/no, true/false)
- **Switch**: Three or more paths (multiple categories)

**Example: Order Priority Routing**
```
                      ┌─ Output 0: 'critical' → Alert on-call team immediately
                      │
Data → Switch Node ───┼─ Output 1: 'high' → Create urgent Jira ticket
                      │
                      ├─ Output 2: 'medium' → Send Slack message
                      │
                      └─ Output 3: 'low' → Log to spreadsheet
```

**Switch Configuration:**
Mode: Rules
Routing Rules:
1. `$json.priority` equals `'critical'` → Output 0
2. `$json.priority` equals `'high'` → Output 1
3. `$json.priority` equals `'medium'` → Output 2
4. Fallback (everything else) → Output 3

**Nested Conditions Example:**
You can chain IF and Switch nodes for complex logic:
```
Data → IF (Is Customer?) 
         ├─ True → Switch (Customer Tier)
         │           ├─ Gold → VIP Treatment
         │           ├─ Silver → Standard Treatment
         │           └─ Bronze → Basic Treatment
         └─ False → Guest Flow
```

content.title: Loops in n8n — Processing Large Datasets
content.explanation:
n8n automatically loops over items — when a node receives 100 items, it processes each one. But sometimes you need more control over looping.

**Automatic Looping (Built-in):**
Most nodes automatically process each item. If 50 items flow into a Gmail node, it sends 50 emails. No configuration needed.

**Loop Over Items Node:**
For cases where you need to:
- Process items in batches (e.g., 10 at a time)
- Add delays between iterations (to avoid API rate limits)
- Implement pagination (fetching page 1, then page 2, etc.)

**Batch Processing:**
APIs often have rate limits (e.g., 'max 100 requests per minute'). The **Split In Batches** node helps:

```
1000 Items → Split In Batches (size: 10)
  ↓ (processes 10 items)
  ↓ (waits)
  ↓ (processes next 10)
  ↓ ... (continues until all 1000 are processed)
```

**Configuration:**
- Batch Size: How many items per batch (e.g., 10)
- The node automatically loops and feeds batches to the next node

**Pagination Pattern:**
When an API returns paginated results:
```
Loop:
  HTTP Request (GET /api/customers?page=1)
  ↓
  Check: Are there more pages?
  ├─ Yes → Increment page number → Loop again
  └─ No → Continue to next node with all collected data
```
content.tip: Always check API rate limits before processing large datasets. Most APIs allow 60-100 requests per minute. Use batch processing with delays to stay within limits.

content.title: Merge Node — Combining Data from Multiple Sources
content.explanation:
The **Merge node** combines data from two or more inputs into a single output. Essential when your workflow has parallel branches.

**Merge Modes:**

**1. Append** — Combine all items from both inputs into one list
```
Input 1: [Alice, Bob]     → Output: [Alice, Bob, Charlie, Diana]
Input 2: [Charlie, Diana]
```

**2. Combine by Position** — Merge items by their index (1st with 1st, 2nd with 2nd)
```
Input 1: [{name: 'Alice'}, {name: 'Bob'}]
Input 2: [{score: 95}, {score: 82}]
Output:  [{name: 'Alice', score: 95}, {name: 'Bob', score: 82}]
```

**3. Combine by Field** — Merge items that share a matching field value (like SQL JOIN)
```
Input 1: [{id: 1, name: 'Alice'}, {id: 2, name: 'Bob'}]
Input 2: [{id: 1, city: 'Mumbai'}, {id: 2, city: 'Delhi'}]
Merge on: 'id'
Output:  [{id: 1, name: 'Alice', city: 'Mumbai'}, {id: 2, name: 'Bob', city: 'Delhi'}]
```

**Project: Combine CRM and Billing Data**
```
                    ┌─ HTTP Request (CRM API) ─────┐
Schedule Trigger ───┤                               ├─ Merge (by customer_id) → Google Sheets
                    └─ HTTP Request (Billing API) ──┘
```

This workflow fetches customer data from two different APIs, merges them by customer ID, and creates a unified report in Google Sheets.

content.title: Project: Process 1,000 Customer Records
content.explanation:
**Scenario:** You have 1,000 customers in a Google Sheet. You need to:
1. Read all records
2. Enrich each with data from an API (which has a rate limit of 30 requests/minute)
3. Write enriched data back to another sheet

**Workflow:**
```
Manual Trigger
  ↓
Google Sheets (Read 1000 rows)
  ↓
Split In Batches (batch size: 10)
  ↓
HTTP Request (Enrich each customer)
  ↓
Wait Node (2 second delay between batches)
  ↓
Loop back to Split In Batches (until all done)
  ↓
Google Sheets (Write enriched data)
```

**Why This Works:**
- 1000 customers ÷ 10 per batch = 100 batches
- 2 second delay between batches
- ~30 requests per minute (within API limits)
- Total time: ~3.5 minutes

Without batching, you would hit the rate limit after 30 requests and get errors for the remaining 970.

content.title: The HTTP Request Node — Your Universal API Connector
content.explanation:
The **HTTP Request** node is the most versatile node in n8n. It can connect to ANY web service that has an API.

**HTTP Methods Explained:**

| Method | Purpose | Example |
|--------|---------|--------|
| **GET** | Read/Fetch data | Get weather, list users, fetch a webpage |
| **POST** | Create/Send data | Create a user, submit a form, send a message |
| **PUT** | Replace/Update data | Update an entire user record |
| **PATCH** | Partially update | Change just the email of a user |
| **DELETE** | Remove data | Delete a record, remove a file |

**Anatomy of an HTTP Request:**

```
Method:  GET
URL:     https://api.example.com/users/123
Headers: {
  "Authorization": "Bearer sk-abc123",
  "Content-Type": "application/json"
}
Query Parameters: ?page=1&limit=10
Body (POST/PUT only): {
  "name": "Alice",
  "email": "alice@example.com"
}
```

**In the n8n HTTP Request node:**
- Method: Select from dropdown (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE)
- URL: The API endpoint
- Authentication: Select the auth type (or use pre-configured credentials)
- Headers: Additional metadata
- Query Parameters: Filters appended to the URL
- Body: Data to send (for POST/PUT/PATCH)

content.title: Authentication Types in HTTP Requests
content.explanation:
Most APIs require authentication. Here are the common types and how to configure them in n8n:

**1. API Key (Most Common)**
The API gives you a key. You include it in a header or query parameter.
```
Header: X-API-Key: your-api-key-here
  OR
Query:  ?api_key=your-api-key-here
```
n8n Config: Authentication → Generic Credential Type → Header Auth or Query Auth

**2. Bearer Token**
Similar to API Key but uses the standard Authorization header.
```
Header: Authorization: Bearer your-token-here
```
n8n Config: Authentication → Predefined → Header Auth with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`

**3. OAuth 2.0 (Google, Slack, GitHub, etc.)**
The most secure method. Requires a setup flow:
1. Create credentials in the service's developer console
2. In n8n, add OAuth credentials with Client ID and Secret
3. Click 'Connect' — a popup lets you authorize
4. n8n stores and auto-refreshes the token

n8n has pre-built OAuth for: Google, Microsoft, Slack, GitHub, Notion, and many more.

**4. Basic Auth**
Username and password encoded in the header.
```
Header: Authorization: Basic base64(username:password)
```
n8n Config: Authentication → Basic Auth → Enter username and password

**Security Rule:** NEVER hardcode API keys in expressions. Always use n8n's Credentials system.
content.tip: When setting up OAuth credentials (Google, Slack), you need to create a project in the service's developer console first. n8n's documentation has step-by-step guides for each service.

content.title: Credentials — Keeping Your API Keys Safe
content.explanation:
Credentials in n8n are the secure containers for your API keys, OAuth tokens, passwords, and other sensitive data.

**Why Credentials Matter:**
- API keys give access to your accounts (Gmail, Slack, OpenAI)
- Leaked keys can result in unauthorized access, data breaches, and unexpected bills
- n8n encrypts credentials at rest (when N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY is set)

**How to Create Credentials:**
1. Go to **Credentials** in the left sidebar
2. Click **Add Credential**
3. Search for the service (e.g., 'Google Sheets')
4. Follow the setup instructions
5. Click **Save**
6. Use the credential in any workflow node

**Credential Types:**

| Type | Setup | Used By |
|------|-------|---------|
| **API Key** | Paste your key | OpenAI, SendGrid, weather APIs |
| **OAuth2** | Click 'Connect' and authorize | Google, Slack, Microsoft, GitHub |
| **Basic Auth** | Enter username + password | Jenkins, some REST APIs |
| **Bearer Token** | Paste your token | GitHub, custom APIs |
| **Header Auth** | Custom header name + value | APIs with non-standard auth |

**Reuse Credentials:**
Once created, a credential can be used across ALL your workflows. Create it once, use it everywhere. If the key changes, update it in one place — all workflows automatically use the new key.

**Environment Variables:**
For self-hosted n8n, you can also reference environment variables in credentials:
```
{{ $env.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
```
This keeps keys out of the n8n database entirely.
content.tip: Create a naming convention for credentials: 'Google Sheets - Marketing Team', 'OpenAI - Production Key', 'Slack - Bot User'. This makes it easy to find and manage them.

content.title: Lesson Summary

content.title: Debugging — Finding and Fixing Problems
content.explanation:
Every workflow will eventually fail. APIs go down, data formats change, rate limits are hit. The difference between a beginner and a pro is how quickly they can find and fix the problem.

**Debugging Tools in n8n:**

**1. Execution Logs**
The Executions page shows every workflow run with:
- ✅ Success or ❌ Error status
- Timestamp and duration
- Click any execution to see the data at each node
- Pin-point which node failed and what data it received

**2. Node Output Inspector**
Click any node after execution to see:
- **Input**: What data the node received
- **Output**: What data the node produced
- **Error**: The exact error message if it failed
- Switch between Table, JSON, and Schema views

**3. Test Individual Nodes**
You can execute just one node (without running the entire workflow):
- Click the node
- Click 'Execute Node'
- See the output immediately
- Great for testing HTTP Request configurations

**4. Console Logging (Code Node)**
In Code Nodes, use `console.log()` to debug:
```javascript
const items = $input.all();
console.log('Number of items:', items.length);
console.log('First item:', JSON.stringify(items[0].json));

// Check appears in the execution's Code Node output
```

content.title: Error Handling — Making Workflows Resilient
content.explanation:
n8n provides powerful error handling features so your workflows recover gracefully instead of crashing.

**1. Continue on Fail**
Enable this on any node to continue the workflow even if that node fails.
- The error is captured in the output data
- Subsequent nodes can check for errors and handle them
- Use case: If email sending fails, still log the data to a spreadsheet

**2. Retry Logic**
Configure nodes to automatically retry on failure:
- Number of retries: 1-5
- Wait between retries: configurable
- Use case: API timeout → wait 5 seconds → try again

**3. Error Trigger Workflow**
Create a separate workflow that runs whenever ANY workflow fails:
```
Error Trigger
  ↓
Slack Node (Send error alert to #alerts channel)
  ↓
Gmail Node (Email the error details to admin)
  ↓
Google Sheets (Log the error for tracking)
```

The Error Trigger receives:
- Which workflow failed
- Which node failed
- The error message
- The input data that caused the failure

**4. Try/Catch Pattern (Code Node)**
```javascript
try {
  // Risky operation
  const result = someFunction();
  return [{ json: { success: true, data: result } }];
} catch (error) {
  return [{ json: { success: false, error: error.message } }];
}
```

**Project: Auto-Recovery Workflow**
```
Schedule Trigger (Every 5 minutes)
  ↓
HTTP Request (Call API) [Continue on Fail: ON, Retry: 3]
  ↓
IF Node (Did it succeed?)
  ├─ True → Process data normally
  └─ False → Slack Alert + Retry in 10 minutes
```
content.tip: Set up an Error Trigger workflow on day one. It takes 5 minutes and will save you from silent failures that go unnoticed for days.

content.title: Building Production-Quality Workflows
content.explanation:
You now know how to build workflows. But there is a huge difference between a workflow that 'works' and one that is production-ready. Let's level up.

**1. Naming Conventions**
- Workflow names: `[Team] Action - Service` → `[Sales] New Lead → CRM + Slack`
- Node names: Verb + Noun → `Fetch Customer Data`, `Send VIP Email`, `Check Is Active`
- Bad: `HTTP Request 1`, `IF`, `Code`
- Good: `GET Weather from wttr.in`, `Is VIP Customer?`, `Calculate Discount`

**2. Folder Organization**
Organize workflows into folders:
```
📁 Sales
   ├── Lead Qualification
   ├── CRM Sync
   └── Follow-up Emails
📁 DevOps
   ├── Server Monitoring
   ├── Deploy Notifications
   └── Incident Alerts
📁 AI Automations
   ├── Email Summarizer
   ├── Content Generator
   └── Support Ticket Classifier
```

**3. Modular Design**
Break complex workflows into smaller sub-workflows that call each other:
- Main Workflow → calls `Validate Data` sub-workflow
- Main Workflow → calls `Enrich Customer` sub-workflow
- Main Workflow → calls `Send Notifications` sub-workflow

Benefits:
- Each sub-workflow can be tested independently
- Reuse sub-workflows across multiple main workflows
- Easier to debug (smaller scope)

**4. Documentation with Sticky Notes**
Add sticky notes to explain:
- What the workflow does (at the top)
- Why specific logic was chosen
- Expected input/output format
- Known limitations or gotchas

content.title: Performance, Versioning, and Production Features
content.explanation:
**5. Performance Optimization**
- Use batch processing for large datasets
- Add Wait nodes to respect API rate limits
- Use the 'Execute Once' option when a node does not need to loop
- Cache frequently-used data (store in a variable, avoid repeated API calls)

**6. Workflow Versioning**
- Export workflows as JSON files regularly
- Store them in a Git repository
- Use meaningful commit messages: `'Added error handling to lead pipeline'`
- Before major changes, export the current version as backup

**7. Activation Checklist**
Before activating a workflow for production:
- ✅ All nodes named clearly
- ✅ Error handling on external API nodes
- ✅ Error Trigger workflow set up
- ✅ Tested with edge cases (empty data, large payloads, special characters)
- ✅ Credentials verified and working
- ✅ Rate limits respected (batch processing where needed)
- ✅ Sticky notes documenting the workflow
- ✅ Exported to Git as backup

**8. Monitoring Active Workflows**
- Check the Executions page daily for the first week
- Set up Slack/email alerts for failures
- Monitor execution duration — increasing times may indicate problems
- Review logs weekly for patterns (same error recurring = systemic issue)

content.title: Practice Project: Smart Lead Management System
content.explanation:
**Welcome to Your Module 2 Capstone Project!**

You have completed all the lessons in this module. Now it is time to combine EVERYTHING into one comprehensive, production-ready workflow.

**Your Mission:**
Build a Smart Lead Management System that captures leads from a website form, validates them, uses AI to qualify them, stores them in a CRM, and notifies your sales team — all automatically.

**Why This Project?**
Lead management is one of the most common automation use cases in business. Companies pay thousands of dollars for tools that do exactly what you are about to build for free.

**The Complete Workflow:**
```
Website Form → Webhook Trigger → Validate Data → Remove Duplicates
  → AI Lead Qualification → Store in Google Sheets → Create CRM Contact
  → Notify Sales Team on Slack → Send Welcome Email → Log Execution
```

**Skills You Will Use:**
- ✅ Triggers (Webhook)
- ✅ Action Nodes (Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack)
- ✅ Expressions (Dynamic content)
- ✅ HTTP Requests (CRM API)
- ✅ AI Integration (OpenAI for lead scoring)
- ✅ Conditional Logic (IF/Switch for routing)
- ✅ Error Handling (Continue on Fail, retries)
- ✅ Data Transformation (Edit Fields, Code Node)
- ✅ Google Workspace Integration
- ✅ Production Best Practices (naming, documentation, monitoring)

content.title: Step 1: Webhook Trigger and Data Validation
content.explanation:
**Step 1A: Set Up the Webhook Trigger**

Create a Webhook that receives lead data from a website form:
```
Webhook Trigger:
  Method: POST
  Path: /new-lead
  Response Mode: Last Node (so the form gets a response)
```

**Expected Input Data:**
```json
{
  "name": "Priya Sharma",
  "email": "priya@techcorp.com",
  "company": "TechCorp",
  "phone": "+91-9876543210",
  "message": "Interested in your enterprise plan for our team of 50 people.",
  "source": "website_contact_form"
}
```

**Step 1B: Validate the Data**

Add an IF node to check for required fields:
```
IF Node: 'Validate Required Fields'
  Conditions (AND):
    - $json.name is not empty
    - $json.email is not empty
    - $json.email contains '@'
  
  True → Continue to next step
  False → Respond with error: 'Missing required fields'
```

**Step 1C: Check for Duplicates**

Query your Google Sheet to check if this email already exists:
```
Google Sheets Node: 'Check Existing Leads'
  Action: Read Rows
  Filter: email = {{ $json.email }}

IF Node: 'Is Duplicate?'
  Condition: $json length > 0
  True → Respond: 'You are already in our system!'
  False → Continue (new lead)
```

content.title: Step 2: AI Lead Qualification
content.explanation:
**Use OpenAI to score and qualify the lead based on their message.**

```
OpenAI Node: 'AI Lead Scorer'
  Model: gpt-4o-mini
  System Prompt:
    'You are a lead qualification expert. Analyze the following lead
    information and return a JSON object with:
    - score (1-100): How likely they are to become a customer
    - tier: "hot" (score > 70), "warm" (score 40-70), "cold" (score < 40)
    - summary: One sentence describing the lead
    - recommended_action: What the sales team should do next'
  
  User Message:
    'Name: {{ $json.name }}
    Company: {{ $json.company }}
    Message: {{ $json.message }}'
```

**Expected AI Response:**
```json
{
  "score": 85,
  "tier": "hot",
  "summary": "Enterprise prospect from TechCorp looking for a team plan for 50 users.",
  "recommended_action": "Schedule a demo call within 24 hours. This is a high-value enterprise lead."
}
```

**Step 3: Route Based on Score**
```
Switch Node: 'Lead Tier Router'
  Rule 1: score > 70 → Hot Lead Path
  Rule 2: score > 40 → Warm Lead Path
  Default → Cold Lead Path
```

**Hot Lead Path:**
→ Slack DM to sales manager: '🔥 HOT LEAD! {{ $json.name }} from {{ $json.company }}'
→ Gmail: Send personalized VIP welcome email
→ Google Sheets: Add to 'Hot Leads' tab

**Warm Lead Path:**
→ Slack #leads channel: '🟡 Warm lead: {{ $json.name }}'
→ Gmail: Send standard welcome email
→ Google Sheets: Add to 'Warm Leads' tab

**Cold Lead Path:**
→ Gmail: Send nurture email sequence
→ Google Sheets: Add to 'Cold Leads' tab

content.title: Step 3: Store, Notify, and Log
Evaluation Criteria and Final Checklist
content.explanation:
**Test Your Workflow:**

Send these test payloads to your webhook and verify each scenario:

**Test 1: Hot Lead**
```json
{"name": "Vikram CEO", "email": "vikram@bigcorp.com", "company": "BigCorp (500 employees)", "message": "Need enterprise plan for 200 users. Budget approved. Want demo this week."}
```
Expected: Score > 70, Slack DM to manager, VIP email

**Test 2: Warm Lead**
```json
{"name": "Sneha Dev", "email": "sneha@startup.io", "company": "Startup.io", "message": "Exploring automation tools for our 10-person team."}
```
Expected: Score 40-70, Slack channel post, standard email

**Test 3: Cold Lead**
```json
{"name": "Test User", "email": "test@gmail.com", "company": "", "message": "Just checking this out"}
```
Expected: Score < 40, nurture email, cold leads sheet

**Test 4: Invalid Data**
```json
{"name": "", "email": "invalid"}
```
Expected: Validation fails, error response returned

**Test 5: Duplicate**
Send the same email twice — second should be caught as duplicate.

**Production Checklist:**
- ✅ All nodes named descriptively
- ✅ Sticky notes documenting each section
- ✅ Error handling on all external nodes
- ✅ Error Trigger workflow configured
- ✅ All 5 test scenarios pass
- ✅ Workflow exported to Git
- ✅ Credentials properly configured

**Congratulations!** You have built a production-ready lead management system that combines triggers, AI, conditional logic, data transformation, multi-service integration, and error handling. You are now ready for Module 3: APIs and AI Integration!
